**The Role of Technology in Modern Education**

Technology is everywhere in school now. Most students in my year carry a laptop to every class, our homework is posted online, and when we don't understand something, the first thing we do is search for it or watch a video. Technology has changed education a lot, even just in the time I've been at school. While it has made learning more flexible and engaging, it also brings problems like distraction and over-reliance, which means it has to be used carefully.

One of the biggest benefits of technology is that it gives students access to almost unlimited information. When my parents were at school, they had to rely on textbooks and the library. Now, if I'm doing a history assignment, I can find primary sources, documentaries and articles from all over the world in minutes. Websites like Khan Academy and Education Perfect also mean that if I miss a lesson or don't understand a topic, I can catch up at my own pace. This is especially helpful for students who learn differently or need more time, because they don't have to keep up with the speed of the whole class.

Technology also makes learning more interactive and interesting. In science, we've used simulations to see experiments that would be too dangerous or expensive to do in the lab. In maths, programs like Desmos let us see how changing an equation changes a graph straight away, which makes it much easier to understand than just working on paper. Quizzes on Kahoot or Quizlet make revision feel more like a game, and I've noticed people in my class actually pay attention more when we use them. Tools like Google Docs also make group work easier, since we can all work on the same document from home.

However, technology also has some serious downsides. The biggest one, from my experience, is distraction. It's very easy to open YouTube or a game when you're supposed to be working, and I'll admit I've done it more than once. Studies have shown that multitasking on devices can make it harder to concentrate and remember information. Another problem is that some students rely too much on technology to do the thinking for them. With AI tools now able to write essays and solve maths problems, some people skip the learning part completely. This might help them finish homework faster, but it doesn't help them understand the content, which becomes obvious in exams.

There's also the issue of fairness. Not every student has a good laptop or reliable internet at home, which can put them at a disadvantage when so much schoolwork is online. Too much screen time can also affect sleep, eyesight and mental health, which are things schools need to think about.

Overall, I think technology plays a really important role in modern education, and it isn't going anywhere. It gives students more ways to learn and makes lessons more engaging. But it works best as a tool to support teachers and learning, not as a replacement for them. Schools need to teach students how to use technology responsibly, and students like me need to take responsibility for using it to actually learn, not just to take shortcuts.

Inflation is the general and sustained rise in the prices of goods and services across an economy, which means each dollar buys less over time. In Australia it is measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI), which tracks the prices of a basket of common household goods and services. The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) aims to keep inflation between 2 and 3 per cent on average over time. Understanding what causes inflation and what its effects are helps explain why it matters so much to households, businesses and governments.

There are three main causes of inflation. The first is demand-pull inflation, which happens when total spending grows faster than the supply of goods and services. For example, if people have more money to spend after a tax cut or a period of strong wage growth, they may bid up the prices of limited goods such as housing. The second is cost-push inflation, which occurs when the costs of producing goods rise, such as higher fuel prices, supply chain disruptions or higher wages that businesses pass on to customers. The third is built-in inflation, sometimes called expectations inflation. If workers and businesses expect prices to keep rising, they will demand higher wages and charge higher prices, and this expectation can become self-fulfilling.

Inflation affects the economy in several ways. The most direct effect is on purchasing power. People on fixed incomes can find that their money no longer covers the same amount of food, fuel or rent. Savers can also lose out if the interest they earn is lower than the inflation rate, because the real value of their money falls. Borrowers may benefit in some cases, because the real value of their debt falls, but only if their income keeps pace with prices.

Inflation also affects interest rates. When inflation is high, the RBA usually raises the cash rate to slow spending and bring prices back under control. This makes mortgages and other loans more expensive, which can reduce demand for housing and other goods. Higher interest rates therefore create real pressure for families with home loans, and they can slow economic growth and sometimes increase unemployment.

On the other hand, a low and stable level of inflation is generally considered healthy, because it encourages spending and investment rather than holding cash. Deflation, where prices fall over time, can be just as damaging, because consumers may delay purchases while waiting for prices to drop further.

In conclusion, inflation is driven by demand pressures, rising costs and expectations, and its effects range from reduced purchasing power to higher interest rates. A moderate level of inflation is normal, but when prices rise too quickly it can cause serious hardship, which is why governments and central banks work to keep it under control.

**Inflation: Causes and Effects**

Inflation is the general rise in prices across an economy over time, which means each dollar buys less than it used to. A small, steady amount of inflation (most central banks, including the Reserve Bank of Australia, aim for around 2–3% a year) is considered healthy. Problems arise when inflation becomes too high, too low or unpredictable.

**Causes**

Economists usually group the causes of inflation into three main types.

*Demand-pull inflation* happens when total demand for goods and services grows faster than the economy can produce them. If consumers, businesses and governments all want to spend more, perhaps because wages are rising, interest rates are low or the government is spending heavily, businesses can raise prices because people are still willing to buy. This is often summed up as "too much money chasing too few goods".

*Cost-push inflation* occurs when the costs of producing goods rise, and businesses pass those costs on to customers. Common triggers include rising oil and energy prices, higher wages, supply shortages or disruptions to supply chains. The jump in inflation in many countries in 2021–22, for example, was partly driven by pandemic supply disruptions and an energy price spike after Russia invaded Ukraine.

*Built-in inflation* (or the wage-price spiral) happens when people come to expect prices to keep rising. Workers ask for higher wages to keep up, businesses raise prices to cover higher wages, and the cycle feeds itself. This is why central banks pay close attention to inflation expectations.

Increases in the money supply can also contribute, especially if a government prints money to fund spending without a matching increase in production. In extreme cases, this can lead to hyperinflation, as seen in Zimbabwe in the 2000s.

**Effects**

The most obvious effect is a fall in purchasing power. If prices rise faster than wages, people's real incomes fall, and they can afford less. This hits people on fixed incomes, such as pensioners and welfare recipients, particularly hard.

Inflation also redistributes wealth. Borrowers can benefit, because the real value of their debt shrinks over time, while savers and lenders lose out if interest rates don't keep pace with rising prices.

High or unpredictable inflation creates uncertainty, making it harder for businesses to plan, set prices and invest. This can slow economic growth. It can also hurt a country's international competitiveness if its goods become more expensive than those of its trading partners.

To bring inflation down, central banks usually raise interest rates. This makes borrowing more expensive and saving more attractive, which reduces spending and eases pressure on prices. However, raising rates too far can slow the economy and increase unemployment, so central banks must strike a careful balance.

In short, inflation reflects the balance between spending, production costs and expectations. Managed well, it is a normal part of a growing economy; left unchecked, it can erode living standards and destabilise the economy.

**Four Days on the Great Ocean Road: Surf, Stacks and Too Many Coffees**

We left Melbourne early on a Saturday morning with a car full of snacks, a playlist that had been argued over for two weeks and a plan to see as much coastline as possible before dark. The Great Ocean Road begins just past Torquay, and within twenty minutes the city had disappeared behind us and the ocean was on our left.

Our first proper stop was Bells Beach, famous for surfing and the Rip Curl Pro. Even on a quiet morning there were surfers out in the waves, bobbing like seals in their wetsuits. We grabbed coffee in Anglesea and kept going along the winding road, which hugs the cliffs and offers a new view around every bend. Keep an eye out for kangaroos on the grassy hills near the coast. We spotted a few grazing right beside the road.

By lunchtime we reached Lorne, a relaxed seaside town with a pier, good bakeries and plenty of cafes. We ate fish and chips on a bench overlooking the water while the gulls tried to steal them. Then we continued past Apollo Bay, where we stayed the night in a small cabin with a view across the bay.

The next morning was the highlight. We drove to Port Campbell National Park, where the limestone stacks known as the Twelve Apostles rise out of the Southern Ocean. There are fewer than twelve left standing after centuries of erosion, which somehow makes them more impressive. Standing at the lookout as the wind picked up, I felt very small. A short walk away, Loch Ard Gorge has a tragic history, and the information panels there are worth reading.

**Tips for anyone planning the trip:**

- Give yourself at least three days if you want to stop properly. Two days is a rushed trip.
- Fill up with fuel in the bigger towns, because petrol stations can be far apart.
- Check the weather and pack layers. The coast can be cold and windy even in summer.
- Book accommodation early in peak season, especially around Apollo Bay and Port Campbell.

The road was built by returned soldiers after the First World War and is often described as the largest war memorial in the world. It is easy to see why people drive it for the views alone.

# Salt, Cliffs and Koalas: Our Great Ocean Road Road Trip

There's a moment, about twenty minutes past Torquay, when the road swings around a headland and the whole coastline suddenly opens up in front of you: sheer cliffs, white surf, and the Southern Ocean stretching out to a horizon that doesn't stop until Antarctica. My partner actually gasped. I nearly missed the turn. And that set the tone for the next four days.

The Great Ocean Road runs roughly 240 kilometres along Victoria's south-west coast, from Torquay to Allansford near Warrnambool. You *could* drive it in a day. Please don't. Here's how we did it, and what I'd tell anyone planning their own trip.

## Day 1: Torquay to Lorne

We left Melbourne mid-morning and stopped first in **Torquay**, the surf capital of Australia, for coffee and a wander. A short detour took us to **Bells Beach**, home of the famous Easter surf competition. Even if you don't surf, standing on the clifftop watching the sets roll in is mesmerising.

Just past Anglesea, we stopped at the **Memorial Arch at Eastern View**, which honours the returned soldiers who built the road after World War I. It's easy to treat it as just a photo stop, but it's worth reading the plaques. The road is the world's largest war memorial, carved by hand with picks, shovels and explosives.

We spent the night in **Lorne**, a lovely seaside town with a great main street. Dinner was fish and chips on the foreshore, being heavily supervised by seagulls.

**Tip:** Erskine Falls is a ten-minute drive inland from Lorne and well worth an early-morning visit before the crowds arrive.

## Day 2: Lorne to Apollo Bay

This was the most spectacular stretch of driving. The road hugs the cliffs so closely that there are sections where it's just mountain on one side and ocean on the other. Use the pull-over bays, both for photos and to let faster locals pass.

At **Kennett River**, we followed the tip from every travel blog ever and walked up Grey River Road looking for koalas. Within five minutes we'd spotted six, mostly asleep in the forks of the gum trees, one looking extremely unimpressed with us. King parrots and crimson rosellas will also land on you if anyone nearby has seeds (please don't feed them).

We reached **Apollo Bay** in the afternoon, a relaxed town with a long sweeping beach. Sunset from Marriners Lookout was one of the highlights of the whole trip.

## Day 3: Cape Otway and the Twelve Apostles

We headed inland through the rainforest of **Great Otway National Park**. The **Maits Rest** rainforest walk is a short loop through towering myrtle beech trees and tree ferns, and it feels like stepping into another world after all that ocean.

Then it was on to **Cape Otway Lightstation**, mainland Australia's oldest surviving lighthouse, with sweeping views and a fascinating history of shipwrecks along what's known as the Shipwreck Coast.

And then, of course, the **Twelve Apostles**. Yes, it's busy. Yes, there are tour buses. And yes, it's still absolutely worth it. Only seven or so of the limestone stacks remain (there were never actually twelve), but watching them glow gold in the late afternoon light is unforgettable. Go at sunset or early morning to avoid the worst of the crowds.

Just down the road, **Loch Ard Gorge** was my personal favourite: a beautiful sheltered cove with a tragic story about the shipwreck of the *Loch Ard* in 1878, where only two of the 54 people on board survived.

We stayed in **Port Campbell**, a tiny, friendly town perfectly placed for exploring the coastline.

## Day 4: The Arch, London Bridge and home

On our last morning, we visited **The Arch**, **London Bridge** (which lost its connection to the mainland in 1990, famously leaving two tourists stranded and needing a helicopter rescue), and **The Grotto**, a sinkhole that frames the ocean like a window.

We finished at **Warrnambool** before cutting back inland to Melbourne via the Princes Highway, which is much faster than retracing the coast.

## Things I'd tell you before you go

- **Take at least three days.** Four is even better.
- **Drive in the Melbourne-to-Warrnambool direction** so you're on the ocean side of the road for better views at the lookouts.
- **Expect slow going.** Winding roads, roadworks and sightseers mean average speeds are lower than you'd think.
- **Watch for wildlife**, especially at dawn and dusk.
- **Book accommodation ahead** in summer and school holidays.
- **Pack layers.** We had sunshine, wind, drizzle and fog, sometimes all in one afternoon.

The Great Ocean Road lives up to the hype, but what stuck with me wasn't just the famous viewpoints. It was the little moments in between: a sleepy koala, chips on the beach, the hush of the rainforest, and that first breathtaking glimpse of coastline just past Torquay. I can't wait to do it again.

There are road trips, and then there's the Great Ocean Road. We spent four days driving this 243-kilometre stretch of Victorian coastline, and I'm still thinking about it.

We started at Torquay, the gateway to the road and the home of Bells Beach. The road from here hugs the cliffs, with the Southern Ocean glittering on one side and thick bush on the other. In Apollo Bay we ate fish and chips on the foreshore, watching pelicans eye our lunch. In the afternoon, we detoured into the Great Otway National Park for the Otway Fly Treetop Walk. Walking through the canopy of ancient mountain ash and giant ferns felt like stepping into another world. We also spotted koalas sleeping in the gum trees along Great Ocean Road near Kennett River. Bring your camera and look up!

This is the postcard stop. We went at sunrise, which I highly recommend because the crowds are smaller and the limestone stacks turn gold. Standing on the lookout with the waves crashing against them, you really feel how old and powerful the coastline is. We also visited Loch Ard Gorge, where the story of the 1878 shipwreck gives the place a sombre feel, and the London Bridge formation, which famously collapsed in 1990.

We finished in the lovely fishing village of Port Fairy, wandering along the wharf, browsing cafes and watching boats come in. It was a quiet end to a big trip.

- Watch for wildlife at dusk, particularly kangaroos.

**The Castle and the Ordinary Australian**

Rob Sitch's 1997 film *The Castle* is one of the most loved Australian films, and it presents a very particular picture of Australian identity. Through the Kerrigan family and their modest house beside Melbourne Airport, the film celebrates ordinary people who stand up to powerful institutions. It shows Australians as humorous, loyal, unpretentious and suspicious of anyone who puts on airs. At the same time, its portrait of who counts as "Australian" is quite narrow.

The Kerrigans are a working-class family, and their house sits at the centre of the story. When the government wants to acquire the land for an airport expansion, Darryl Kerrigan refuses to sell. The house is not valuable to him for its money but for what it means to his family. This reflects a deep Australian value: the things you have built with your own hands matter more than wealth or status.

Humour and mateship run throughout the film. Darryl's awkward but warm dealings with his family and neighbours make the audience laugh, but they also show loyalty. The famous line "It's the vibe of the thing" captures the idea that feeling and character can matter more than polished argument. Rob Sitch's 1997 film *The Castle* is one of Australia's best-loved comedies, but beneath its jokes lies a thoughtful portrait of Australian identity. Through the story of Darryl Kerrigan, a tow-truck driver who fights to stop his family home from being compulsorily acquired for an airport expansion, the film celebrates values that many Australians see as central to who they are: the importance of home and family, a belief in the "fair go", and a deep suspicion of authority and pretension. At the same time, the film quietly acknowledges a more complicated side of national identity through its references to Indigenous land rights.

At the heart of *The Castle* is the idea that home is more than property. Darryl's house at 3 Muncaster Road sits beside an airport runway and under power lines, and it is filled with odd extensions and DIY projects. To outsiders, it is unremarkable, even ugly. But to Darryl, it is priceless. His famous line, "It's not a house, it's a home," captures a belief that a person's sense of identity is tied to the place where they raise their family and build their memories. The film reflects the long-standing Australian dream of home ownership, but it presents it not as a matter of wealth or status, but of belonging. The Kerrigans' home is valuable precisely because of the love and effort that has gone into it.

The film also celebrates the ordinary "battler", a figure who has long been central to Australian identity. The Kerrigans are working-class, unsophisticated and endlessly enthusiastic about simple things, from Darryl's pride in his wife Sal's cooking ("What do you call this, love?") to his delight in a bargain from the Trading Post. Sitch invites us to laugh with the Kerrigans rather than at them. Their optimism, loyalty and contentment are presented as admirable qualities. In a country that often prides itself on being egalitarian, the film suggests that true worth lies not in money or education but in character, family and a good heart.

Closely linked to this is the idea of the "fair go", the belief that everyone deserves to be treated equally, no matter their background. When the government and a large corporation try to take the Kerrigans' home, Darryl refuses to accept that powerful interests can simply override ordinary people. His fight reflects a typically Australian distrust of authority and bureaucracy. His inexperienced lawyer, Dennis Denuto, famously struggles to make a legal argument, falling back on, "It's the Constitution, it's Mabo, it's justice, it's law, it's the vibe." While played for laughs, the line captures something real: an instinctive sense of fairness that many Australians feel matters more than legal technicalities. The case is eventually taken up by Lawrence Hammill, a retired barrister who, moved by Darryl's sincerity, argues it all the way to the High Court, and wins on the basis that the property was not acquired on "just terms".

Importantly, the film also connects the Kerrigans' struggle to Indigenous experiences of dispossession. This moment is brief, and some critics argue the film only scratches the surface of a much deeper issue. However, it does suggest that Australian identity cannot be fully understood without acknowledging the history of land and belonging that came before colonisation. In this way, the film hints that the "fair go" Australians value has not always been extended to everyone.

Ultimately, *The Castle* represents Australian identity as warm, humble and fiercely loyal to family and home. It celebrates the battler who stands up to the powerful, the importance of fairness, and the joy of simple pleasures. Through its humour, it gently reminds audiences of the values many Australians hold dear, while also prompting them to consider whose stories of home and belonging have been overlooked. More than twenty-five years after its release, the film's enduring popularity suggests that its vision of Australia, and its "vibe", still resonates.
